title: VAYU KISHORE VS. STATE OF KARNATAKA

paras.text:
2026 INSC 1130
Page 1 of 26
REPORTABLE
IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CIVIL APPEAL NO. 13785 OF 2026
(@SPECIAL LEAVE PETITION (C) NO. 4163 OF 2024)
 VAYU KISHORE ...Appellant
VERSUS
 STATE OF KARNATAKA & ORS. ...Respondents
WITH
SPECIAL LEAVE PETITION (C) NO. 37143 OF 2026
(@SPECIAL LEAVE PETITION (C) DIARY NO. 13855 OF 2026)
ABHILASHA SHARMA ...Petitioner
VERSUS
VAYU KISHORE ...Respondent
ORDER
CIVIL APPEAL NO. 13785 OF 2026
(@SPECIAL LEAVE PETITION (C) NO. 4163 OF 2024)
1. Leave granted.
2. "Marriage is a wonderful institution, but who wants to live in an
institution?"
(Groucho Marx)

Page 2 of 26
3. This appeal arises from the judgment and order passed by the
High Court of Karnataka dated 20.12.2023 in W.P.H.C No. 43 of
2023, by which the Writ Petition preferred by the Appellant before
us, seeking a writ of Habeas Corpus, came to be dismissed.
I. FACTS AND THE IMPUGNED JUDGEMENT
4. The facts in brief giving rise to this appeal are as under:-
a. The Appellant is a US citizen, whereas Respondent No.4 had
relocated to the USA on a Fiancé Visa, sponsored by the
Appellant. On 05.05.2018, the Petitioner and Respondent
No. 4 solemnised and registered their marriage in South
Brunswick, New Jersey, USA. No wedding ceremony took
place in India, and the parties never resided together as
husband and wife within the territory of India. The parties
set up the Matrimonial Home in Mountain View, California,
USA.
b. Respondent No.4 is a doctor by profession and, on her
relocation to the USA, cleared the US medical licensing
examination, with the intent to practice medicine there. She
also acquired a 10-year permanent residency (Green Card)
of the USA.
c. In the wedlock between the Appellant and Respondent No.
4, a daughter was born on 19.05.2019 in the USA. She is
also a citizen of the USA.
d. After the birth of the child, it appears that the matrimonial
relations between the parties went sour. The Appellant and
Respondent No.4 separated, and Respondent No.4 and the

Page 3 of 26
child moved out of the house and started living in a separate
house in California.
e. While the parties were in the US, the Respondent No. 4
invoked the jurisdiction of the Superior Court of California,
County of Contra Costa, USA ("Superior Court of
California") and preferred a petition seeking dissolution of
marriage on the ground of "irretrievable breakdown of
marriage". To put it in other words, "irreconcilable
differences".
f. The proceedings instituted by the Respondent No. 4 led to
the issuance of summons by the Superior Court of
California, which contained the Automatic Temporary
Restraining Orders, restraining both the parties, i.e., the
husband and the wife, from removing the minor daughter
from the jurisdiction of California or applying for a new or
replacement passport without prior written consent of the
other party or an order of the Court.
g. It also appears that sometime in 2022, the Respondent No.4
again invoked the jurisdiction of the Superior Court of
California by preferring a custody petition. She prayed for
sole and legal custody of the minor daughter along with child
support and spousal support. She further prayed that the
Appellant, as father, should only have visitation rights.
h. The Superior Court of California, after hearing both parties
and keeping in mind the best interests of the child, passed
an order dated 25.08.2022 granting joint custody and
shared parenting to both parents, with an equal 50:50 time
share on a 4-3-3-4 schedule. The Court observed that

Page 4 of 26
nothing on record indicated that the time share should be
anything other than 50:50. The order further stipulated that
the child could not be taken out of the State of California
without the written consent of the other parent or an order
of the court. Having regard to the incomes and needs of the
parties and the child, the Court also directed the Petitioner
to pay child support of USD 1,095 per month and temporary
spousal support of USD 2,116 per month to Respondent No.
4, thereby safeguarding the welfare of both the minor child
and Respondent No. 4. A review hearing on these directions
was listed for 02.12.2022.
i. It is not in dispute that both parties complied with the order
of the Superior Court of California for about two weeks. On
08.09.2022, however, Respondent No. 4 left the USA for
India with the child. Despite the specific directions in the
order dated 25.08.2022, Respondent No. 4 is alleged to have
surreptitiously removed the minor daughter from the State
of California, in violation of that order.
j. It is the case of the Respondent No.4 that after reaching
India, she sent an e-mail on 10.09.2022 to the Appellant
informing that she left the USA along with the child and had
travelled to India. The aforesaid developments led the
Appellant to file a police complaint on 20.09.2022 in the USA
against his wife, i.e., the Respondent No. 4, for removal of
the child.
k. On 02.12.2022, the Superior Court of California, at the
review hearing that was already scheduled, recorded a
violation of the order dated 25.08.2022 referred to above and
directed the Respondent No. 4 to immediately return the

Page 5 of 26
child to the Appellant's physical custody in California. The
Court also ordered that the Appellant would have sole
custody for the purposes of obtaining and maintaining a
passport for the minor child, and all future child
custody/visitation between the minor child and Respondent
No. 4 shall be professionally supervised until further orders.
All financial support, including the spousal support and
child support granted, was suspended until the Respondent
No.4 came into compliance with the Court's orders.
l. The Appellant, thereafter, was left with no other option but
to prefer a writ petition in the High Court of Karnataka and
prayed for the following reliefs:-
"a. Issue an appropriate writ, order or direction in the
nature of Habeas Corpus to Respondent Nos. 1, 4
and 5 to immediately trace and produce the minor
child, Miss Vindhya Kishore before this Hon'ble Court
and deliver her custody to the Petitioner-father so as
to repatriate her to USA in compliance with the order
dated 02.12.2022 passed by the Foreign Court;
b. Issue an appropriate writ, order or direction in the
nature of Habeas Corpus to Respondent No. 3 to
trace Respondent No. 6 and through her produce
Miss Vindhya Kishore before this Hon'ble Court, in
view of the illegal detention of Miss Vindhya by
Respondent No. 6 and violation of Custody Order
dated 25.08.2022 passed by the Foreign Court;
c. Issue appropriate directions to Respondent No. 6
to restore and handover legal and physical custody
of Miss Vindhya Kishore to the Petitioner;
d. Issue appropriate directions to Respondent No. 6
to facilitate Miss Vindhya 's safe return to USA in
compliance with the order dated 02.12. 2022 passed
by the Foreign Court;
e. Issue appropriate directions to Respondent No. 6
to handover the requisite documents such as

Page 6 of 26
passport and other travel documents of the minor
child, Miss Vindhya Kishore, which are in her
custody, to the Petitioner- father in order to facilitate
Miss Vindhya 's return to USA;
f. Issue appropriate directions to Respondent No. 2 to
provide requisite information pertaining to
immigration of Miss Vindhya to India;
g. Allow costs of the present petition in favour of the
Petitioner; and
h. Pass such other order or further orders and
directions as this Hon'ble Court may deem fit and
proper in the facts and circumstances of the case and
in the interest justice."
m. The High Court, after considering the various issues
involved, dismissed the writ petition.
n. In such circumstances, as referred to above, the appellant
is here before us with the present appeal.
5. The High Court, after taking into account the necessary facts and
submissions, framed the following two issues for its consideration:
(a) Whether the child's custody with Respondent No.4 is illegal;
and (b) Whether the Appellant is entitled to the child's custody and
her return to the USA?
6. The reasoning of the High Court in dismissing the Writ Petition
may be summarised as follows:
a. Relying on the decision of this Court in Tejaswini Gaud v.
Shekhar Jagdish Prasad Tewari, reported in (2019) 7
SCC 42, the High Court held that, in child custody matters,
a writ of habeas corpus is maintainable only where it is
shown that the detention of a minor child by a parent or
others is illegal and without any authority of law.

Page 7 of 26
b. Placing reliance on Nithya Anand Raghavan v. State (NCT
of Delhi), reported in (2017) 8 SCC 454, the High Court
observed that the mere existence of a foreign court order
directing the mother to produce the child before it does not,
by itself, render the child's custody with the mother
unlawful. In such situations, the High Court must examine
whether returning the child to the country from which he or
she was removed would serve the child's interests or would
harm them. That assessment has to be made on the totality
of the facts and circumstances, and the order of the foreign
court must yield to the welfare of the child.
c. Applying these principles, the High Court held that the
child's custody with Respondent No. 4 was not illegal. It
reasoned that Section 6 of the Hindu Minority and
Guardianship Act, 1956 makes the custody of a female child
below the age of five years with her mother lawful, and that
the order of the US court did not, by itself, alter this position.
d. Having so held, the High Court turned to the best interests
of the child. It concluded that it would be in the best interest
of the child, a four-year-old girl, to remain in her mother's
custody. The following factors appear to have weighed with
the High Court in reaching this conclusion:
i. During the interaction in chambers, the child's
demeanour "firmly disclosed" that she was comfortable
only with her mother;
ii. The Appellant did not act immediately and filed the
Writ Petition nearly eight months after the child was
brought to India, by which time she had begun

Page 8 of 26
attending school in Jamshedpur. In matters involving
emotional attachment and bonding, the High Court
regarded eight months as a fairly long period;
iii. No evidence had been brought on record to show that
Respondent No. 4 had caused the child any harm.
e. Lastly, relying on Vasudha Sethi v. Kiran V. Bhaskar,
reported in 2022 SCC OnLine SC 43, the High Court
observed that a writ court dealing with a petition for habeas
corpus cannot direct a parent to leave India and go abroad
with the child, since such a direction, if issued against the
parent's wishes, would offend her or his right to privacy.
Given the bitter hostility between the parties, the High Court
therefore held that it would not be appropriate to compel
Respondent No. 4 to move to the USA. It left it open to the
parties to work out their rights to custody and visitation
separately.
7. Before proceeding further, we may note that when this matter first
came up for hearing, we thought it fit to explore an amicable
resolution of the disputes before proceeding to hear the matter on
merits. We took up the matter in the Committee Room on not less
than ten occasions and passed several orders over a period of time.
We tried our best to persuade all concerned to bury their
differences, keeping only the interest of the child in mind. On two
occasions, the Appellant travelled to India and appeared before us
in the Committee Room, where we interacted with him.
Unfortunately, since the parties could not reach any consensus,
we are left with no option but to decide the matter on its merits.
II. SUBMISSIONS ON BEHALF OF THE PARTIES

Page 9 of 26
8. Mr. Mukul Rohatgi and Ms. Meenakshi Arora, learned Senior
Counsel, along with Mr. Prabhjit Jauhar, learned counsel
appearing for the Appellant, made the following submissions:
a. The High Court committed an egregious error in dismissing
the Writ Petition and, thereby, declining to issue the writ as
prayed for.
b. Respondent No. 4, having invoked the jurisdiction of the
Superior Court of California by preferring a custody petition
with respect to the minor child and having obtained an order
of joint custody and shared parenting, could not have
surreptitiously left for India in violation of that very order.
c. Having married the Appellant, settled in the USA and chosen
to raise a family there, Respondent No. 4 was not expected,
over trivial differences, to take the extreme step of leaving for
India one fine day without the Appellant's knowledge. This
was all the more so because her own parents were then
residing in the USA. While her parents are now in India, the
Appellant's parents, who are also US citizens, continue to
reside in the USA, presently in New Jersey.
d. The child, being a citizen of the USA, should not be deprived
of her upbringing there, more particularly her education.
e. Reliance was placed on two decisions of this Court: (i)
Rajeswari Chandrasekar Ganesh v. State of Tamil Nadu
and Others, reported in (2023) 12 SCC 472; and Yashita
Sahu v. State of Rajasthan and Others, reported in
(2020) 3 SCC 67.

Page 10 of 26
f. To demonstrate his bona fides, the Appellant offered the
following undertakings: (i) he would arrange a separate
accommodation for Respondent No. 4 near his residence in
the USA and bear all expenses for it, including rent; (ii) he
would assist Respondent No. 4 in having her Green Card,
which has since lapsed, restored; (iii) he would provide
Respondent No. 4 monthly financial assistance of USD 3,200
per month as ordered by the Superior Court of California,
and bear all her travel and other miscellaneous expenses; (iv)
he would not take any legal steps against Respondent No. 4
in respect of the alleged violation of the order dated
25.08.2022, and would cooperate in any other proceedings
initiated against her in the USA, so as to restore family life.
g. In short, the Appellant is more than willing to save the
marriage and revive the marital ties in the larger interest of
the child.
h. In such circumstances, it was prayed that the appeal be
allowed and appropriate directions be issued in the larger
interest of all concerned, more particularly the child.
9. Ms. Malavika Rajkotia, learned counsel appearing for Respondent
No. 4, vehemently opposed the appeal and made the following
submissions:
a. The High Court committed no error, much less an error of
law, in passing the impugned judgment and order. It
addressed itself to the two vital questions that arose for its
consideration, keeping in mind the hard facts of the case,
more particularly the reality on the ground.

Page 11 of 26
b. Respondent No. 4 has been in India with the child for almost
four years. Although the child may be in touch with the
Appellant through video calls, the Appellant has not, as a
father, shown any inclination to revive the marital ties with
Respondent No. 4 in the larger interest of the child.
c. On the aspects of comity of courts and the welfare of the
minor child, it needs to be noted that India is not a signatory
to the Hague Convention. It is important to appreciate the
plight of an Indian woman who marries, moves abroad
thousands of miles away from her parents, and thereafter
finds herself in difficulty in a foreign country.
d. Respondent No. 4 does not wish to deprive the Appellant of
a role in the child's upbringing. She is more than willing for
the child to begin visiting her father in the USA over a period
of time. According to the learned counsel, the Appellant is
also most welcome to visit India and spend time with his
daughter.
e. In such circumstances, the learned counsel prayed that the
appeal, being devoid of merit, be dismissed.
III.ISSUE FOR CONSIDERATION
10. Having heard the learned counsel appearing for the parties and
having perused the material on record, the only question that falls
for our consideration is whether the High Court committed any
error in passing the impugned judgment and order.

Page 12 of 26
IV. APPROACH TO BE ADOPTED
11. Cases such as these, where two parents each seek custody of their
child, and a court of a foreign country has already dealt with this
aspect in some manner, have been coming before this Court time
and again. Yet, the decision in such cases does not become any
easier. This is because they involve deeply emotional and sensitive
issues, the answer to which cannot be straitjacketed into a legal
formula. No such formula can exist, for in such matters precision
is either absent or cannot be sought. However, before we turn to
which way the answer in the present case should go, it is still
important to broadly understand the factors that this Court has
held must be borne in mind when dealing with such cases.1
12. At the outset, it is too late in the day to urge that a writ of habeas
corpus is not maintainable merely because the child is in the
custody of the other parent. No such contention has been
advanced by learned counsel on either side. However, when a
petition for habeas corpus is brought in the context of child
custody, and the contest is between two parents, we believe the
focus of the inquiry must shift from what the writ ordinarily stands
for. Generally, the writ asks a simple question: is the detention
legal or illegal? That question serves well in most situations. But
in a dispute between two parents, a debate on legality takes us
nowhere. Each parent may well have an equal and lawful claim to
the child's custody. In fact, the purpose of the petition in such
cases is not to test the legality but to give the court a means by
1 See, Ravi Chandran (Dr.) (2) v. Union of India & Ors, (2010) 1 SCC 174; Yashita Sahu
v. State of Rajasthan, (2020) 3 SCC 67; Elizabeth Dinshaw v. Arvand M. Dinshaw, (1987)
1 SCC 42; Dhanwanti Joshi v. Madhav Unde, (1998) 1 SCC 112; Sarita Sharma v. Sushil,
(2000) 3 SCC 14, Nithya Anand Raghavan v. State (NCT of Delhi), (2017) 8 SCC 454;
Lahari Sakhamuri v. Sobhan Kodali, (2019) 7 SCC 311; and Rajeswari Chandrasekar
Ganesh v. State of Tamil Nadu, (2023) 12 SCC 472.

Page 13 of 26
which it may determine what is best for the welfare of the child.
This is also why this Court has recognised time and again that the
decision in such petitions rests not on the legal rights of the
parties, but on the welfare of the child.
13. It follows that where two parents are involved, the threshold
condition for entertaining a petition for habeas corpus need not be
illegal detention as such. It may instead be the wrongful
deprivation of one parent's right to custody brought about by the
actions of the other.2 This threshold condition, however, serves
only to get a foot in the door. Once it is crossed, the matter is no
longer decided based on the rights of the parents.
14. The question then is: once the threshold condition is met, on what
basis is such a petition for habeas corpus to be decided? We are
primarily concerned with answering this question in cases with
facts such as the one before us, i.e., the contest is between two
parents, a court of a foreign country ( where the parties had set up
their matrimonial home) has already passed an order on custody,
and the child has been brought to India, or kept in India,
seemingly in violation of that order. This Court has, on several
occasions, dealt with petitions for habeas corpus arising in
precisely these circumstances. We do not wish to burden this
order by discussing each of those decisions at length. Instead, we
think it fit to cull out the broad principles that can be readily
gathered from a reading of those judgments.3
15. First and foremost, the welfare of the child is the paramount
consideration in every such case, whatever orders the courts of
another country may have made. Put differently, a court in this
2 Tejaswini Gaud v. Shekhar Jagdish Prasad Tewari, (2019) 7 SCC 42. 3 Supra note 1.

Page 14 of 26
country, when exercising its jurisdiction, cannot blindly follow the
order of a foreign court and act merely as an executing court
16. This position rests on two foundations. The first is that once the
court is seized of the matter, it exercises its parens patriae
jurisdiction. That jurisdiction obliges it to consider and assess the
matter for itself, through the lens of the child's welfare. The
second, as noted above, is that the decision in such cases turns
not on the legal rights of the parties but on the welfare of the child.
The same emphasis on welfare over legal entitlement runs through
our statutes on custody and guardianship.4 They make clear that
a person otherwise entitled to custody or guardianship need not
be granted it if that would not be for the welfare of the child. There
is thus no ambiguity in the fact that an order of a foreign court
must yield to the welfare of the child.
17. The necessary consequence of the paramountcy of the child's
welfare, and of a foreign order yielding to it, is simple. A parent's
disobedience of a foreign order does not, by itself, require the court
to give automatic effect to that order. Nor can the remedy of habeas
corpus be invoked merely to enforce the directions of a foreign
court.
18. Secondly, the paramountcy of the child's welfare does not mean
that the order of a foreign court is to be disregarded. In deciding
what the welfare of the child requires, the court must form its own
independent judgment. In doing so, however, it must give proper
weight to the order of the foreign court. Comity of courts may not
4 See Rajeswari Chandrasekar Ganesh v. State of Tamil Nadu, (2023) 12 SCC 472.

Page 15 of 26
require that such an order be enforced, but it does require that the
order be given grave consideration.
19. What constitutes proper weight will depend on the circumstances
of each case. The weight to be given to the order of a foreign court
may turn on a few factors, such as: (i) the nature of the order,
including whether the foreign court examined the best interests of
the child on the merits, whether both parties were heard, and who
instituted the proceedings before it; (ii) the time that has elapsed
since the order was passed; and (iii) whether circumstances have
changed in the interim. No single factor is decisive. It is the
combination of these factors that must be considered. Proper
weight, therefore, is not a matter of mathematical precision. It is a
matter of the court's considered assessment of how far the foreign
order reflects the welfare of the child.
20. Thirdly, and closely connected to the first two principles, is the
question of the nature of the inquiry the court must undertake.
The court must independently consider the welfare of the child,
and in considering it must assign proper weight to the order of the
foreign court. But before the court undertakes that exercise, it
must first decide whether the case calls for a summary inquiry or
an elaborate one. In a summary inquiry, the court proceeds on the
footing that the welfare of the child is best served by following the
order of the foreign court. The child is therefore returned to the
country from which the child was removed, unless it is clearly
shown that such return would be harmful to the child. In an
elaborate inquiry, the court does not stop at the foreign order. It
takes the order into account, but goes on to examine for itself
where the welfare of the child truly lies. The distinction was

Page 16 of 26
explained by this Court in Dhanwanti Joshi v. Madhav Unde,
reported in (1998) 1 SCC 112, in the following terms:
29. [...] In the case of (a) a summary inquiry, the court
would return custody to the country from which the child
was removed unless such return could be shown to be
harmful to the child. In the case of (b) an elaborate inquiry,
the court could go into the merits as to where the
permanent welfare lay and ignore the order of the foreign
court or treat the fact of removal of the child from another
country as only one of the circumstances. The crucial
question as to whether the Court (in the country to which
the child is removed) would exercise the summary or
elaborate procedure is to be determined according to the
child's welfare. The summary jurisdiction to return the
child is invoked, for example, if the child had been removed
from its native land and removed to another country
where, maybe, his native language is not spoken, or the
child gets divorced from the social customs and contacts to
which he has been accustomed, or if its education in his
native land is interrupted and the child is being subjected
to a foreign system of education, - for these are all acts
which could psychologically disturb the child. Again the
summary jurisdiction is exercised only if the court to which
the child has been removed is moved promptly and quickly,
for in that event, the Judge may well be persuaded that it
would be better for the child that those merits should be
investigated in a court in his native country on the
expectation that an early decision in the native country
could be in the interests of the child before the child could
develop roots in the country to which he had been removed.
Alternatively, the said court might think of conducting an
elaborate inquiry on merits and have regard to the other
facts of the case and the time that has lapsed after the
removal of the child and consider if it would be in the
interests of the child not to have it returned to the country
from which it had been removed. In that event, the
unauthorised removal of the child from the native country
would not come in the way of the court in the country to
which the child has been removed, to ignore the removal
and independently consider whether the sending back of
the child to its native country would be in the paramount
interests of the child. [...]
[Emphasis Supplied]

Page 17 of 26
21. The following two aspects emerge from the above extract: First, the
two inquiries do not differ in their central aim. Both are directed
at determining the course of action that best promotes the welfare
of the child. Where they differ is in how closely the court examines
welfare. Second, the promptness with which the court is
approached, and the extent to which the child has since developed
roots in the country to which the child was removed, weigh heavily
in that choice.
22. However, the term "elaborate inquiry", when used in the context
of a petition for habeas corpus, only indicates that the court's
inquiry will be more exhaustive than a summary inquiry. It does
not mean that the court may travel beyond the limits that
ordinarily govern it in such petitions. The court cannot lose sight
of the fact that the only question to be decided in such a petition
is whether or not the writ ought to issue. The question is not to
decide fully and finally with whom custody of the child must lie.
The scope and nature of proceedings in a petition for habeas
corpus simply do not permit that. It follows that any observations
made in such proceedings must be confined to that limited
question. They should not influence the court that later considers
the question of custody in substantive proceedings, where all
aspects must be examined on their own merits.
23. Fourthly, the expressions "welfare of the child" and "best interests
of the child" must be understood in their widest sense. Welfare is
not to be measured by money or physical comfort alone. In this
regard, it is instructive to refer to the observations of Hardy Boys,
J. in Walker v. Walker & Harrison, as extracted and relied upon by
this Court in Dhanwanti Joshi (supra):

Page 18 of 26
"Welfare is an all-encompassing word. It includes material
welfare, both in the sense of adequacy of resources to
provide a pleasant home and a comfortable standard of
living and in the sense of an adequacy of care to ensure
that good health and due personal pride are maintained.
However, while material considerations have their place
they are secondary matters. More important are the
stability and the security, the loving and understanding
care and guidance, the warm and compassionate
relationships, that are essential for the full development of
the child's own character, personality and talents."
24. In Rajeswari Chandrasekar Ganesh (supra), wherein one of us,
J.B. Pardiwala, J., was a part of the Bench, adopted the same
approach and observed as follows:
"127. We would therefore hold that in the case at Bar, the
dominant consideration to which all other considerations
must remain subordinate must be the welfare of the child.
This is not to say that the question of custody will be
determined by weighing the economic circumstances of the
contending parties. The matter will not be determined
solely on the basis of the physical comfort and material
advantages that may be available in the home of one
contender or the other. The welfare of the child must be
decided on a consideration of these and all other relevant
factors, including the general psychological, spiritual and
emotional welfare of the child. It must be the aim of the
court, when resolving disputes between the rival claimants
for the custody of a child, to choose the course which will
best provide for the healthy growth, development and
education of the child so that he or she will be equipped to
face the problems of life as a mature adult."
[Emphasis Supplied]
25. Apart from the requirement that welfare be understood in its
widest sense, there are no hard and fast rules in assessing the
welfare of the child. Everything depends on the facts and
circumstances of the case, and it is the totality of those facts and
circumstances that must be taken into consideration. No fixed
formula can be laid down. This Court, in Lahari Sakhamuri v.

Page 19 of 26
Sobhan Kodali, reported in (2019) 7 SCC 311, set out the
following factors that may be considered in assessing the welfare
of the child with respect to each parent:
"49. The crucial factors which have to be kept in mind by
the courts for gauging the welfare of the children equally
for the parent's can be inter alia, delineated, such as (1)
maturity and judgment; (2) mental stability; (3) ability to
provide access to schools; (4) moral character; (5) ability to
provide continuing involvement in the community; (6)
financial sufficiency and last but not the least the factors
involving relationship with the child, as opposed to
characteristics of the parent as an individual."
[Emphasis Supplied]
26. Lastly, while the welfare of the child is the governing
consideration, it is equally important not to lose sight of the
principle that a wrongdoer ought not to gain an advantage from
their own wrong. Comity of courts is a healthy doctrine, and the
orders of a competent foreign court deserve respect. A parent who
removes a child, or retains a child, in disregard of such an order
should not ordinarily be permitted to benefit from having done so.
27. We must be careful, however, in stating how this principle
operates. It is not to be balanced against the welfare of the child,
for that would take away the primacy that welfare must always
enjoy. In many cases, the welfare of the child will clearly point to
one course. There, the inquiry ends, and the wrongdoing is not a
factor in consideration at all. But at times, the prevailing
circumstances may be so puzzling that it becomes difficult to
weigh the conflicting considerations and decide which way the
scales tip. The welfare of the child may be met more or less equally
whichever way the court decides. It is in such cases, and only after
the welfare of the child has been fully considered, that the court
may legitimately have regard to the fact that one parent has acted

Page 20 of 26
in disregard of the order of a competent court. Welfare is not
displaced in such cases. This approach has been followed by this
Court in a plethora of instances, where, while retaining the
primacy given to welfare considerations, this Court also took into
account this aspect to determine which way to tilt.
V. APPLICATION TO THE FACTS AT HAND
28. With this approach in mind, we may now turn to the matter before
us. The High Court held that the custody of the child with the
Respondent No.4 was lawful. Whether custody retained in breach
of an order of a court in the USA can, strictly speaking, be called
lawful is not a question on which we consider it necessary to spend
much time. As explained above, in cases such as the present, the
threshold condition does not depend on establishing that the
detention is illegal. It is equally satisfied where one parent has
been wrongfully deprived of their right to custody by the actions of
the other. This is because the primary focus in such cases is not
on a strict assessment of legality, but on the welfare of the child.
The High Court was, therefore, right to examine the matter on the
touchstone of what is in the best interests of the child,
notwithstanding its view that the custody of the mother was
lawful.
29. The High Court did not expressly state whether it was undertaking
a summary or an elaborate inquiry. It is evident from its judgment,
however, that it undertook an elaborate inquiry. We are also of the
view that the present case does not lend itself to being decided
based on a summary inquiry. The Appellant approached the High
Court within eight months of the child being retained in India. The
matter has since travelled to this Court, where time was also spent

Page 21 of 26
in attempts to resolve the dispute amicably. As a result, the child
has now been residing in India for nearly four years. In such
circumstances, a decision based on a summary inquiry would not
be warranted.
30. In assessing the best interests of the child, the High Court, as
noted above, relied on the delay of eight months, the absence of
any material showing harm to the child in the custody of the
mother, and the child's demeanour, which "firmly disclosed" that
she was comfortable only with her mother. We do not think these
considerations are sufficient to hold that the welfare of the child
could be served only by her remaining with her mother, and not
with her father.
31. The child has lived only with her mother for the past four years.
It is only natural, then, that her demeanour would reflect a wish
to remain with her mother. Given her tender age, it is
unfortunately not possible to ascertain her own wishes in any
meaningful sense, much less to solely rely upon them. Similarly,
the High Court may have been correct in observing that no harm
was shown to have been caused to the child in the custody of
Respondent No. 4. But on a perusal of the record, especially the
custody proceedings initiated by Respondent No.4 in the USA, it
appears to us that there is nothing substantial to show that the
child would suffer harm if placed in the custody of her father. In
these circumstances, neither consideration can reasonably be said
to tilt the scales in favour of Respondent No. 4.
32. Nor do we think that a period of eight months was sufficient for
the child's roots in India to become so firmly established that her
welfare lay only in remaining here with her mother. This is all the
more so because she was only about three years of age when

Page 22 of 26
Respondent No. 4 brought her to India. It is true that she has now
spent nearly four years here, and that her early formative years
have been spent in this country. Even so, we do not think this
clearly establishes that her welfare can be served only by
remaining in India with her mother. On the other hand, the child
is a citizen of the United States and is entitled to all the benefits
that such citizenship carries. That, in our view, makes a strong
case for her to continue her life in the United States, particularly
when nothing on record suggests that an upbringing there would
hamper her progress or would not be in her interests. We believe
that the child, being a USA citizen, should grow up in the USA and
receive an education in the USA.
33. While we are of the view that the welfare of the child lies in
continuing her life in the United States, we are conscious that this
is not a case in which the considerations point overwhelmingly in
one direction. The child has, after all, spent her early formative
years in India with her mother. It is in these circumstances that
the manner in which the child came to be in India assumes
relevance, and lends further support to the view we have taken.
34. It is not disputed that the Appellant and Respondent No. 4
solemnised their marriage in the United States and set up their
matrimonial home there. In fact, both the divorce and the custody
proceedings in the United States were instituted by Respondent
No. 4 herself. A perusal of the custody order dated 25.08.2022
shows that it was passed after hearing both parties and after
taking into account the best interests of the child. Yet, barely two
weeks after that order was passed, Respondent No. 4 brought the
child to India, in clear breach of the conditions it contained.
Nothing on record suggests that her circumstances were so grave

Page 23 of 26
or frightening that she was left with no option but to take the child
out of the USA.
35. In these circumstances, the comity of courts, and the principle
that a party ought not to benefit from their own wrong, tilt the
scales in favour of the Appellant. We must, however, clarify once
again that our decision does not rest on these considerations
alone. The welfare of the child has remained the governing
consideration throughout. We have had regard to these principles
only to further substantiate and support our conclusion that the
welfare of the child would be better served in the USA.
36. The appeal, therefore, deserves to be allowed, and the child must
be returned to the United States into the custody of the Appellant,
subject to the directions that follow.
